texts.facts: This criminal appeal is preferred by the appellant under Section 29 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, calling in question the legality, correctness and propriety of the order dated 18-03-2021 passed by the MMTC-V, Bengaluru, on I.A. No.1 in Crl. Misc. No.40/2021, whereby the trial court has (i) directed deletion of Respondent No.2 from the array of parties, and (ii) declined to exercise interim jurisdiction under Section 23(2) of the Act in relation to protection against alienation, return of Stridhan, monetary relief and educational expenses of the hearing-impaired minor child. 2. The appellant is the legally wedded wife of Respondent No.1. It is the consistent and categorical case of the appellant that after marriage she was subjected to grave physical, verbal, emotional and economic abuse at the hands of Respondent No.1 and also at the active instigation and participation of Respondent No.2, who is the elder sister of Respondent No.1. 3. The appellant has specifically pleaded that Respondent No.2 was not a distant or passive relative, but was personally and physically involved in acts of domestic violence, including manhandling, pulling of gold chain, instigating assaults and exerting constant psychological pressure upon the appellant. It is further pleaded that the appellant was compelled to part with her entire Stridhan and gold ornaments, which were purchased from her own earnings and meant for the security of herself and her minor daughter. 4. It is further pleaded that the appellant had invested her hard-earned money in the construction of the schedule residential house, which was subsequently let out on rent and the rental income was enjoyed exclusively by Respondent No.1. It is the specific allegation that, in order to defeat the legal and residential rights of the appellant, Respondent No.1, in collusion with Respondent No.2, executed an Agreement of Sale in favour of Respondent No.2, thereby attempting to divest the appellant of her right to residence and financial security. 5. The appellant further pleaded that she lost her employment due to the pandemic and that her minor daughter is hearing-impaired, requiring constant medical treatment and special education. It is her grievance that throughout the subsistence of the marriage, Respondent No.1 has not contributed even a single rupee towards the maintenance, education or medical needs of the child. No.1 under Section 23(2) of the Act seeking interim protection against alienation of the schedule property, interim monetary relief, return of Stridhan, litigation expenses and educational expenses of the minor child. 7. The learned Magistrate, by order dt.18-03-2021, without issuing notice to Respondent No.2 and without undertaking any prima-facie adjudication on the allegations against her, held that: i) The prayer restraining alienation of property is "civil in nature"; ii) There was no shared household between the appellant and Respondent No.2; iii) Hence the petition was not maintainable against Respondent No.2; iv) Consequently, Respondent No.2 was directed to be deleted from the array of respondents. 8. In all the 1st Respondent incurred marriage expenses of Rs.3,00,000/- out of his savings. After the marriage the 1 Respondent taken a rental house at Peenya Dasarahalli, Bengaluru, in the year 2006 and started his marital life with Appellant with pond of hope to lead happy marital life. The marital life of petitioner and 1st Respondent is started at Dasarahalli Bengaluru, after the marriage the Appellant wished and intended to persuade the higher education, the 1 Respondent agreed to fulfill the intention of Appellant and agreed to support to extend all the financial assistance to the Appellant to complete her higher education. At the time of marriage in the year 2006 to 2011 the 1st Respondent getting monthly salary of Rs.13000/- to 14,000/- and out of his salary amount managed the rent, food etc., and by taking hand- loans the 1st Respondent in the year 2007 joined the Appellant to Diploma Electrics and Electronics three years course in Chronic Foundation Institute situated at WOC Road, Indl. Town, Rajajinagar, Bengaluru. The 1 Respondent having pond of love and affection towards his wife dedicated his life and earnings and succeeded provide diploma course to the Appellant. During last/third year of diploma the Appellant conceived and at the time of 8th months pregnancy the Appellant constrained to go to her parents house for delivery and due to 8th months pregnancy two subjects on left out and the Appellant went to her parents house for delivery. During pregnancy the 1st Respondent looked after the welfare of Appellant and even she went to her parents house for delivery the 1st Respondent taken care of the Appellant. 12. The Respondent No.1 submits that, the he admitted the Petitioner in 'Ananya Hospital' Rajajinagar for delivery and the 1 Respondent incurred Rs.50,000/- for delivery expenses, the Appellant gave a birth to female child on 28.08.2009 after discharge the Appellant went to her parents house for post delivery at that time the respondent lost his job and had several financial problems, thereafter the respondent taken rent house at Peenya Dasarahalli Bengaluru and the Appellant and Respondent with child stayed in the rented house, the Petitioner joined to work in a private company. After Appellant joined to the work she completely changed her behavior and attitude towards Respondent and she used to pick up quarrels everyday and she used to abuse to the Respondent on one or other reasons, the Respondent completely avoided and refused to have physical relationship with the respondent and she was saying that she don't want to have any relationship with respondent. The Appellant in order to suppressed the illegal relationship tried to abortion and even after till today she is have illegal relationship with said Sunil and for name sake only the 1 Respondent as husband and in order to create sympathy and suppressed illegal relationship filed the present petition and also filed petition u/s-125 of Cr.P.C. in Crl. The Appellant assaulted and abused to the 1 Respondent and threatened to him in this regard the 1st respondent given police complaint. The 1st Respondent will produced the phone call conversation by way of CD and chips/pen drive. The 1st Respondent being husband to the Appellant lost his respect in the society and suffered mentally and physically. The Sunil and his friends negotiated with the Appellant to prepare a plan to kill the 1 Respondent and the same is recorded will be produced by the 1st Respondent. , all the alleged the copies of purchasing gold are all created. 20. With regard to contents made in para 6 of the Petition that, somewhere in June 2017. As suggested by the Respondent No.1. Appellant agreed to shift to live with the sister of Respondent No. 1 named Yashoda [Respondent No.2), who is living in her own three storied house at the address mentioned in the cause title, i.e., Nandini Layout, Maruthi Nagar at Bengaluru. Appellant and Respondent No.1 took a portion of the house owned by Respondent No.2 and her husband Ramakrishna on rent are true and correct. The Respondents in the above case specifically denied all allegations and contents made in para iiil, iv 7 to 10 of the petition and denied the allegations and contents made in para 11 to 23 and denied all the grounds and denied the relief sought in the petition.
texts.arguments: The 1st Respondent submits that the Respondent sister viz Puttamma requested the Respondent to marry her daughter and convinced all the brothers and sisters to marry her daughter with Respondent, the Respondent also agreed to marry the Appellant. At the time of marriage negotiation the Appellant parents requested to the Respondent to bear all the marriage expenses to the 1 Respondent since they have no any income, the 1 Respondent considering the poor financial status of the petitioner parents agreed to incur all the marriage expenses out of his savings. Accordingly the 1 Respondent given one gold Mangalya chain, gold Thali, one Necklace, pair of ear rings and incurred all the marriage expenses. 15. The Respondent No.1 submits that he collected the phone call conversations of Appellant and Sunil, as per phone call conversation the Appellant and Sunil discussed with vulgar words and the phone call conversation very clearly discloses the illegal sexual relationship of Appellant and Mr. Rajalakshmi J vs K Lokesha on 19 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190454000/ 16. The Respondent No.1 submit that the Appellant have no any moral rights to file the present petitions and have no any rights to claim any relief before this Hon'ble Court. The Appellant is earning more than Rs.40,000/- every month and the same is admitted in the petition and she can able to maintain herself and to maintain her daughter. The 1st Respondent lost physical and mental balance due to the Appellant character and lost his job moreover unable to concentrate on his job hence the Respondent unable to maintain himself. There is no any domestic violence meted out by the Appellant at any point of time and she herself caused and given domestic violence and mental torture and physical torture to the 1st Respondent. The Appellant intentionally left the house and staying separately with continuation her illegal relationship with Sunil. The Appellant continuously deserted and neglected since from 2010 till today and for last 10 years there is no physical 17. With regard to contents made in para 3 of the Petition that, the Respondent no.1 is the husband, the respondent No.2 is the own sister is not correct as the 5th MMTC Court is rejected the petition as against Respondent no.2, the minor daughter is not at all have any physical complication and the same is does not constitute domestic violence moreover there is no any domestic violence occurred on the appellant at any point of time, all the allegations made in 3 para of the petition are false and denied by the Respondents. The Respondent submits the true facts herein above that apart the Appellant being qualified more than Respondent is capable to earn moreover as admitted in the appeal/petition the petitioner is earning Rs.40,000 to 50,000/-every month and capable to maintain herself. On these grounds, the respondent prayed this Court to dismiss the Appeal filed u/s-29 of Protection of Woman under Domestic Violence Act, 2005 with exemplary cost in the interest of justice and equity. 26. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vimlaben Ajitbhai Patel v. Vatslaben Ashokbhai Patel, (2008) 4 SCC 649, has held that: "Economic security and right to shelter are integral facets of the right to life under Article 21." 27. Therefore, any judicial approach that mechanically excludes a woman from statutory protection under the Act must be tested against the constitutional obligation of the Courts to protect dignity, shelter and livelihood of women. Rajalakshmi J vs K Lokesha on 19 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190454000/ 9 28. This reasoning stands directly overruled by the Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in: Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora, (2016) 10 SCC 165, wherein the expression "adult male" in Section 2(q) was struck down and it was held that: "Any relative of the husband, whether male or female, can be proceeded against under the Act if domestic violence is alleged." 29. Thus, after Hiral Harsora, sisters-in-law are fully amenable to jurisdiction under the Act. This position has been repeatedly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in: Smt. Renuka v. Smt. Saroja, 2019 SCC OnLine Kar 1796, where it is held that: "Deletion of female relatives at the threshold is impermissible when allegations disclose active participation in domestic violence." 30. In the present case, the appellant has made specific, categorical and direct allegations against Respondent No.2 of physical assault, instigation, and collusion in depriving her economic rights. 31. The trial court gravely erred in holding that the restraint against alienation is "purely civil in nature". This finding reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of Section 3(iv) of the Act, which defines "economic abuse" to include: "alienation of assets whether movable or immovable in which the aggrieved person has an interest or is entitled to use by virtue of the domestic relationship". 32. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in V.D. Bhanot v. Savita Bhanot, (2012) 3 SCC 183, clearly held that: "Deprivation of proprietary and residential rights constitutes one of the most serious forms of domestic violence." 33. Further, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Kishore Kumar v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2023) 10 SCC 420, it is authoritatively laid down that: "Economic abuse includes systematic deprivation of financial and proprietary entitlements and cannot be reduced to mere non-payment of maintenance." Rajalakshmi J vs K Lokesha on 19 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190454000/ 10 34. The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in Smt. Lakshmi v. Ramesh, 2020 SCC OnLine Kar 5149, held that: "The Magistrate has full jurisdiction under Sections 18 and 19 of the Act to restrain alienation of property when such alienation defeats the residential rights of the aggrieved woman." 35. In the present case, the appellant has pleaded that: a) She invested money in the construction of the property; b) The rental income is enjoyed by Respondent No.1; c) The alienation is in favour of Respondent No.2; d) The transfer is intended to defeat her residential rights. Thus, the act complained of is not a neutral civil transaction, but a weaponized economic act intended to domestically dis-empower the aggrieved woman, which squarely falls within Section 3(iv). 36. The rigid insistence by the trial court on the continued existence of a shared household is also legally unsustainable. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in:Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja, (2021) 1 SCC 414, clarified that: "A shared household is not confined to a house where the husband and wife lived together last, but includes any household where the aggrieved woman lived in domestic relationship." 37. Thus, absence of present cohabitation does not bar jurisdiction against a relative who commits domestic violence. 38. The appellant produced receipts evidencing gold purchases under Annexure-G. The failure of the trial court to even advert to these documents amounts to patent non- application of mind. Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rashmi Chopra v. State of U.P., (2019) 15 SCC 357, held that: "Stridhana is the absolute property of the woman and unlawful retention constitutes a continuing offence and economic abuse." 39. Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in Smt. Manjula v. Ramesh, ILR 2021 KAR 3254, has further held that interim orders on Stridhana cannot be mechanically refused. 40. The minor child is hearing-impaired, dependent entirely on the appellant and requires continuous education and medical care. The father has statutory and constitutional obligations under Article 21 and Article 39(f). In Gaurav Nagpal v. Sumedha Nagpal, (2009) 1 SCC 42, the Supreme Court held that: "The welfare of the child is the paramount consideration, overriding all technical objections." 41. The trial court's silence on this aspect amounts to constitutional neglect. Rajalakshmi J vs K Lokesha on 19 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190454000/ 11 42. Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shalu Ojha v. Prashant Ojha, (2019) 7 SCC 200, has held that: "Section 23 empowers the Magistrate to pass immediate protective orders based on prima- facie satisfaction." 43. Instead of adopting this protective approach, the trial court virtually conducted a mini-trial at the interim stage, which is legally impermissible.
